items.raw_snippet:
Artificial intelligence is rewriting the rules of mergers and acquisitions, forcing dealmakers to reconsider what makes businesses valuable. Javi Rodriguez, Global Head of Strategy at KPMG International, explains why AI defensibility is becoming a critical factor in assessing acquisition targets.

Q: Why is AI moving up the M&A agenda?

AI is changing how businesses generate value across software, engineering and professional services. [...] AI assessment needs to begin during acquisition screening rather than appearing as an additional exercise near the end of due diligence.

Buyers should evaluate both opportunities and threats. AI could accelerate growth, improve productivity and strengthen customer relationships. Equally, it could erode revenues, weaken margins or undermine established market positions. [...] Dealmakers therefore need to examine not just current capabilities but management’s capacity to adapt as technological and commercial conditions evolve, even before the transaction is completed.

Ultimately, AI is making competitive advantage more difficult to measure precisely when accurate valuation matters most.

items.raw_snippet:
The value of global mergers and acquisitions is soaring close to a record level this year as companies rush to gain a competitive edge from artificial intelligence, according to Apollo Global Management Chief Economist Torsten Sløk. [...] ### Dive Insight:

The fixation on AI has spurred dealmaking well beyond technology into companies involved in sectors essential for the AI build-out, including data centers, power generation, power grid infrastructure, cooling and connectivity, Sløk said.

“AI is the trigger of the AI boom, but it is lighting up far more than tech,” he said, noting that dealmaking involving utilities and energy companies posted a record first half. [...] Among the largest AI-focused deals, SpaceX in June bought Anysphere, the creator of AI-coding agent Cursor, for $55 billion, according to Mergermarket.

Although the value of deals soared during the first nine months of this year, the volume declined by 1% to 32,419 transactions, according to ION Analytics.

items.title: Strategy Is Not Conscience: The Moskovitz Perspective, Artificial Intelligence, and the Moral Imperatives of Military Command and Control > Institute for National Strategic Studies > View Publications
items.snippet: In his timely and provocative essay, The Danger of Unregulated Artificial Intell...
items.raw_snippet:
In his timely and provocative essay, The Danger of Unregulated Artificial Intelligence: A Commentary on the Instantiation of Strategy Over Conscience, Dr. Peter Moskovitz articulates a fundamental distinction that should be central to any prudent consideration of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in military and national security applications: the distinction between the computational optimization of strategy and the genuinely moral deliberation required to determine whether a [...] AI systems, by contrast, can optimize specified objectives without independently appreciating the moral significance of the means employed or consequences produced.

This distinction becomes particularly dangerous when the operational objectives of an AI system are narrowly defined, inadequately bounded, or inadvertently misaligned with broader human values and institutional obligations. [...] Finally, responsibility must remain traceable across the human-machine enterprise. The incorporation of AI into decision processes must not create ambiguity regarding who authorized an action, upon what information, under which constraints, and with what foreseeable consequences.
